newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing - Euro will need time to establish itself.
newsitem.headline: Issing - Euro will need time to establish itself.

text.p: Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Tuesday that some uncertainty about the quality of the planned single currency would linger even after the members of the euro had been decided in 1998.
That uncertainty would only disappear gradually, Issing said in a speech.
"So even in the most favourable scenario the euro is likely to need time before it can establish itself on international markets," Issing told a conference on the euro in Frankfurt.

He said past experience had shown that structural changes in international currency systems happened very slowly, as was seen when the U.S. dollar replaced the British pound as a world reserve currency.
He also said it was not yet certain that the euro would be able "seamlessly" to take over the mark's role as an international currency.

The euro's "inner quality" would determine its international role and depended on political and economic factors such as confidence in its stability, how developed financial markets in Europe are and the economic and political weight of the euro zone.
Issing said it remained to be seen whether the launch of the euro, scheduled for January 1, 1999, will benefit or harm other reserve currencies.

"On the one hand, shifts out of DM investments into dollar investments are possible. Many assume this applies to the introductory phase in particular, when the reputation of the euro will first have to be built," Issing said.
On the other hand the worldwide demand for currency reserves as a whole could fall, Issing said.
Euro member countries would have less need for reserves to maintain the European Monetary System and to cushion themselves from unforeseen developments, Issing said.

Assuming all European Union members eventually join the euro at some stage, foreign trade as a proportion of EU members' gross domestic product will on average fall to less than 10 percent from about 23 percent, similar to the level in the U.S., Issing said.

The euro members' vulnerability to global exogenous shocks will decline while the problem of assymetrical shocks -- those which affect individual euro member states differently -- will emerge with full force.
"This will primarily have consequences for goods and labour markets and for economic, fiscal and wage policies. But it will also possibly affect the significance of currency reserves."

Issing said the decline in demand for reserves would probably hit the dollar in particular since the U.S. currency had always played a major role in currency intervention within the European Monetary System.
"What net effect will result from the different effects cannot be said a priori."
